subtopic_detail: Structuring induction and maintenance therapy for repeated culture proven vaginal yeast infection
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old teacher who has had five episodes of vulval itch with a thick white discharge in the past twelve months. Each episode was confirmed on high vaginal swab, each cleared within days of a topical antifungal, and each returned within six to ten weeks.

She uses no soap on the vulva, wears cotton underwear and has not used antibiotics for two years. She has one regular partner who has no symptoms. Her most recent swab grew Candida albicans with sensitivity to azoles, and no bacterial pathogen or trichomonas was detected. She is not pregnant, takes no immunosuppressant medication, and her glycated haemoglobin and human immunodeficiency virus serology are both normal.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with satellite lesions, thick adherent white discharge, vaginal pH 4.2
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab growing Candida albicans sensitive to azoles, glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Recommend oral lactobacillus probiotics daily with dietary sugar restriction
options.rationale: Probiotics and dietary measures have not been shown to prevent recurrence in controlled trials and delay effective suppressive therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: A single oral fluconazole dose taken at the onset of each future episode
options.rationale: Episodic treatment is appropriate for sporadic infection and is what she has effectively been doing, since it clears each attack without altering the pattern of recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries used twice weekly for the next six months
options.rationale: Topical maintenance is an alternative when oral therapy is contraindicated, such as in pregnancy, but adherence is poorer and it is not the first choice for a non pregnant woman (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Treat her partner with a topical antifungal at the same time as each episode
options.rationale: This is not a sexually transmitted infection and randomised evidence shows partner treatment does not reduce recurrence in the woman (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Oral fluconazole induction over one week then weekly maintenance for six months
options.rationale: Four or more culture proven episodes in a year defines recurrent disease, and induction followed by six months of suppressive weekly dosing is what breaks the cycle, with about half remaining free of recurrence after maintenance ends (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as four or more symptomatic episodes in twelve months, and confirmation by culture matters because a large proportion of women self treating for thrush have another cause entirely, including dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and vulvodynia. Speciation is part of that confirmation, since non albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, respond poorly to azoles and need alternative agents such as intravaginal boric acid or nystatin. Predisposing factors worth excluding are diabetes, immunosuppression, high dose oestrogen exposure and repeated antibiotic courses, but most women with recurrent disease have none of them. Treatment is a defined induction course followed by six months of weekly suppression, and around half of women remain in remission after suppression stops while the remainder relapse and may need longer maintenance. Fluconazole is avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy, where topical therapy is used instead.
key_points: Four or more culture proven episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease.
Confirm by culture and speciate, since non albicans species respond poorly to azoles.
Induction followed by six months of weekly oral suppression is the standard regimen.
Partner treatment does not reduce recurrence; this is not a sexually transmitted infection.
Exclude diabetes and immunosuppression, though most women have no predisposing condition.
explanation.pearls: Candida glabrata is the species to suspect when azole therapy repeatedly fails despite good adherence, and it is treated with intravaginal boric acid pessaries or nystatin rather than by escalating the fluconazole dose.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choosing between a history indicated suture and ultrasound surveillance in recurrent midtrimester loss
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the maternal foetal medicine clinic seeing a 31 year old woman at 13 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had three previous pregnancies that ended at 19, 21 and 20 weeks, and no living children.

On each occasion she described pressure and a watery discharge over a day or two, and was found to be several centimetres dilated with bulging membranes before she had any contractions. There was no bleeding, no fever and no abdominal pain on any of the three occasions, and placental histopathology after the second loss showed no chorioamnionitis. Her current pregnancy is a singleton with normal first trimester screening and a nuchal translucency within normal limits. Today's transvaginal cervical length is 34 mm with no funnelling and a mid vaginal swab shows normal flora.

data_table.Examination: Uterus consistent with dates, cervix closed on speculum examination, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal cervical length 34 mm with no funnelling, mid vaginal swab normal flora, first trimester combined screening low risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her cervix in this pregnancy?

options.text: Serial cervical length scans from 16 weeks with a suture if the length falls below 25 mm
options.rationale: Ultrasound indicated cerclage is the strategy for one or two previous losses or a shortened cervix without a definite history, and with three painless midtrimester losses the surveillance approach risks catching the cervix once it is already dilating (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: History indicated cervical cerclage placed now while the cervix is still long
options.rationale: Three consecutive painless midtrimester losses with progressive dilatation and no bleeding, contractions or infection is the pattern for which a history indicated suture at 12 to 14 weeks reduces preterm birth, and it is placed before any shortening occurs (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: Vaginal progesterone nightly from 16 weeks with no scans and no suture
options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth in women with a short cervix found on scan, but it has not been shown to substitute for a suture where the history itself establishes cervical insufficiency (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

options.text: Cervical pessary inserted at 16 weeks and removed at 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Pessary trials have produced inconsistent results and it is not an established alternative to a suture in a woman with this history (Source: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline).
source_refs: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline

options.text: Reduced activity with pelvic rest and weekly review through the second trimester
options.rationale: Bed rest and activity restriction do not prevent preterm birth and carry real harms including venous thromboembolism, deconditioning and lost income (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage).

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis built on a pattern of painless progressive dilatation in the midtrimester leading to loss or extreme preterm birth, in the absence of labour, abruption or infection. The three cerclage categories are distinguished by what triggers them: history indicated sutures are placed electively at 12 to 14 weeks on the basis of previous losses, ultrasound indicated sutures follow a shortened cervix on surveillance, and rescue sutures are placed when dilatation with exposed membranes is found. Placental histopathology and the absence of contractions, bleeding and fever matter because infection driven and abruption driven losses have a different mechanism and do not benefit from a suture. First trimester aneuploidy screening is performed before an elective suture so that a chromosomally abnormal pregnancy is not sutured. Complications include membrane rupture, infection and cervical laceration if labour begins with the suture in place, so the suture is removed at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier if labour starts.
key_points: Painless progressive dilatation without labour, bleeding or infection defines the clinical pattern.
History indicated cerclage is placed at 12 to 14 weeks after three or more midtrimester losses.
Ultrasound indicated cerclage follows a short cervix in women with a less definitive history.
Complete first trimester screening before placing an elective suture.
Remove the suture at 36 to 37 weeks, or sooner if labour or membrane rupture occurs.
explanation.pearls: The suture must come out at the onset of labour: leaving it in place while a woman contracts against it is what produces cervical laceration and annular detachment, so removal instructions travel with the woman in her handheld record.

sources.label: RCOG: Cervical cerclage green top guideline
Safer Care Victoria: Preterm birth prevention

subtopic_detail: Timing birth by peak bile acid concentration in cholestasis of pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 33 weeks and 2 days. For twelve days she has been unable to sleep because of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet, and she has scratched the skin of her forearms until it bled.

There is no rash apart from linear excoriations. She has no right upper quadrant pain, headache or visual disturbance. Blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. Foetal growth is on the 45th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and the cardiotocograph is normal. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and a liver ultrasound shows normal ducts and no gallstones.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 156 U/L (less than 30 in pregnancy), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (2-24), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue the pregnancy to 39 to 40 weeks with weekly bile acid measurement
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk in this condition rises sharply once peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L, and continuing to term accepts the period of highest risk without benefit (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: A peak bile acid concentration at or above 100 micromol/L defines severe disease for which birth is recommended at 35 to 36 weeks, and ursodeoxycholic acid is offered in the interim for maternal itch though it does not alter perinatal outcome (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Deliver today by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
options.rationale: Birth at 33 weeks exposes the baby to substantial prematurity for a risk that becomes material closer to term, and this condition is not in itself an indication for caesarean birth (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Prescribe emollients with a sedating antihistamine at night and review at term
options.rationale: Symptomatic measures are reasonable adjuncts for itch, but relying on them and deferring the timing decision ignores the bile acid concentration that drives the perinatal risk (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis).

options.text: Commence oral dexamethasone for pruritus and continue routine antenatal care
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is less effective than ursodeoxycholic acid for itch in this condition and repeated maternal corticosteroid exposure for a symptomatic indication is not justified (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus that is worst on the palms and soles and at night, without a primary rash, and is confirmed by raised serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases. The clinically important variable is the peak bile acid concentration, because the association with stillbirth is concentrated in the severe group: risk is close to background below 40 micromol/L, modestly raised between 40 and 99, and rises steeply at 100 micromol/L and above. Timing of birth is therefore stratified, with birth around 38 to 39 weeks for mild disease, 36 to 37 weeks for moderate disease and 35 to 36 weeks for severe disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves maternal itch and biochemistry but a large randomised trial showed no reduction in perinatal death or preterm birth, so it is offered for symptoms rather than as protection. Other causes of itch and deranged liver tests, including pre-eclampsia, acute fatty liver, viral hepatitis and gallstone disease, are excluded before the diagnosis is settled, and the condition recurs in a majority of subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: Peak bile acid concentration stratifies risk and drives the timing of birth.
Bile acids at or above 100 micromol/L define severe disease with birth at 35 to 36 weeks.
Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itch but does not reduce stillbirth or preterm birth.
Itch of palms and soles without a primary rash is the characteristic presentation.
Exclude pre-eclampsia, acute fatty liver, viral hepatitis and biliary obstruction before settling the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Bile acids need not be fasting for the timing decision, and it is the highest value recorded across the pregnancy rather than the most recent one that determines which gestation band the woman falls into.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Follow up interval for an incidental simple adnexal cyst in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman referred after an ultrasound arranged for one episode of right sided abdominal pain that settled the same day and has not returned.

She has regular 29 day cycles with no bloating, early satiety or weight loss, and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Abdominal and pelvic examination is normal. The pelvic ultrasound was performed on day 7 of her cycle, and the findings for both ovaries and the uterus are recorded in her file.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no palpable mass, no ascites, cervix and uterus normal on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with a 6 cm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst, thin smooth wall, no solid areas or septations, no internal vascularity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Annual ultrasound surveillance while the cyst remains unchanged and asymptomatic
options.rationale: A simple unilocular anechoic cyst between 5 and 7 cm in a premenopausal woman carries a negligible risk of malignancy, so yearly imaging to confirm stability is sufficient and intervention is reserved for growth, symptoms or a change in morphology (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding
options.rationale: The malignancy index is designed for postmenopausal assessment, and CA125 rises with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and pelvic infection in premenopausal women, generating false alarms for a clearly benign morphology (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to obtain a histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Surgery on a benign appearing cyst removes normal ovarian cortex with it and reduces ovarian reserve in a woman who may want to conceive, for no diagnostic gain (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress and resolve the cyst
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception prevents new functional cysts forming but randomised evidence shows it does not hasten resolution of a cyst that is already present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in six weeks and discharge her if the cyst has resolved
options.rationale: A short interval rescan is the approach for cysts under 5 cm that are likely to be functional, and it is a near miss here because a 6 cm cyst warrants confirmation of stability over a longer horizon rather than a single early rescan (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts).

explanation.summary: Most adnexal cysts found in premenopausal women are functional and resolve without intervention, and the ultrasound morphology rather than the size alone determines how they are managed. A simple cyst is unilocular, anechoic, thin walled and avascular with no solid component or papillary projection, and this appearance is associated with a very low malignancy risk at any premenopausal size. Simple cysts under 5 cm generally need no follow up, those between 5 and 7 cm are followed with yearly imaging, and those above 7 cm are difficult to assess fully with ultrasound and prompt further imaging or a surgical opinion. Features that change the pathway are solid areas, papillary projections, thick septations, internal vascularity, ascites and any suggestion of peritoneal disease. Sudden severe pain with a known cyst raises torsion or rupture and is a separate acute problem needing prompt assessment, and larger cysts are more prone to torsion.
key_points: Morphology, not size alone, determines the management of an adnexal cyst.
Simple cysts under 5 cm in premenopausal women need no follow up.
Simple cysts of 5 to 7 cm are followed with yearly imaging.
CA125 is unreliable premenopausally and is not used to assess a clearly simple cyst.
Solid areas, papillary projections, thick septations, vascularity or ascites change the pathway.
explanation.pearls: Warn her about torsion rather than about cancer: a cyst of this size carries a real risk of sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, and that presentation needs assessment within hours, whereas the malignancy risk here is close to nil.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer clinical guidelines

subtopic_detail: Acting on endometrial thickness in a woman with bleeding after the menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58 year old woman who had two episodes of light red vaginal bleeding in the past three weeks. Her last menstrual period was four years ago and she has taken no hormone therapy.

She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with a small amount of blood at the external os and no visible lesion, and her cervical screening test six months ago detected no oncogenic human papillomavirus. Bimanual examination finds a mobile, normal sized, non tender uterus with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrium measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion, normal ovaries and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with blood at the external os, mobile normal sized uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with endometrial thickness 9 mm and no focal lesion, cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the bleeding reflects atrophic change and review if it recurs
options.rationale: Atrophy is the commonest cause of bleeding after the menopause but it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and an endometrium of 9 mm requires tissue before that label can be applied (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months to see whether it thins
options.rationale: Repeat imaging delays diagnosis without adding information, since the measurement has already crossed the threshold that mandates sampling (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

options.text: Measure serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the reference range
options.rationale: CA125 has no role in the assessment of endometrial pathology and a normal value would falsely reassure in the presence of a thickened endometrium (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines

options.text: Commence a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control the bleeding
options.rationale: Progestogen therapy is a treatment for confirmed hyperplasia without atypia, and inserting it before a histological diagnosis risks treating an unrecognised carcinoma (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines

options.text: Arrange endometrial sampling, proceeding to hysteroscopy if sampling is inadequate
options.rationale: Bleeding after the menopause with an endometrium above 4 mm requires histology, and outpatient sampling is the first line with hysteroscopy and directed biopsy when the sample is insufficient or bleeding persists (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding).

explanation.summary: Bleeding after the menopause carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma, and that risk alone justifies investigating every episode rather than the recurrent ones only. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first line test, and an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a woman not taking hormone therapy has a high negative predictive value that allows conservative management if bleeding does not recur. Above that threshold, or with persistent or recurrent bleeding whatever the thickness, histology is required. Outpatient sampling with a suction device is well tolerated and diagnoses most cancers, but it samples blindly, so an insufficient sample or a focal lesion on imaging leads to hysteroscopy with directed biopsy. Obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, late menopause, tamoxifen use and Lynch syndrome all raise the risk, and obesity operates through peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue. Most endometrial cancers present at an early stage precisely because they bleed early.
key_points: Every episode of bleeding after the menopause is investigated, not only recurrent episodes.
An endometrium of 4 mm or less without hormone therapy has a high negative predictive value.
Above 4 mm, or with persistent bleeding at any thickness, histology is required.
Blind sampling misses focal lesions, so hysteroscopy follows an inadequate sample or a focal finding.
Obesity, diabetes, nulliparity, tamoxifen and Lynch syndrome are the principal risk factors.
explanation.pearls: The 4 mm threshold applies only to women not taking hormone therapy: on sequential hormone therapy the endometrium is measured in the week after the progestogen phase, and on tamoxifen the ultrasound appearance is unreliable altogether so hysteroscopy is the investigation of choice.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer clinical guidelines
